drivingQuestion: When the intent behind a consecration or pledge is uncertain or unfulfillable as stated, must the object be interred, and may a pledged coin be put to other use?
outcomeNote: The objection to Rav is answered by rereading what the baraita's case teaches, and R' Zeira's distinction is cancelled by Rava's לא שנא.

segments.he: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: גּוֹי שֶׁהִפְרִישׁ תְּרוּמָה מִכִּרְיוֹ, בּוֹדְקִין אוֹתוֹ, אִי בְּדַעַת יִשְׂרָאֵל הִפְרִישָׁהּ — תִּינָּתֵן לַכֹּהֵן, וְאִם לָאו — טְעוּנָה גְּנִיזָה, חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא בְּלִבּוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם.
segments.en: § «Rav Yehuda says» that «Rav says:» With regard to «a gentile who separated teruma from his pile» of grain, «one examines him» to determine his intent. «If he separated it with» the «intent» that it be like the teruma of «Jews, it should be given to a priest. If not, it requires interment,» as «we are concerned» that «perhaps his heart was» directed «toward Heaven,» i.e., his intent was to consecrate it to the Temple and he did not want it to be given to a priest. Since there is uncertainty with regard to his intent, nothing can be done with that produce.

segments.he: מֵיתִיבִי: גּוֹי שֶׁהִתְנַדֵּב קוֹרָה, וְשֵׁם כָּתוּב עָלֶיהָ — בּוֹדְקִין אוֹתוֹ, אִם אָמַר: ״בְּדַעַת יִשְׂרָאֵל הִפְרַשְׁתִּיהָ״ — יָגוֹד וְיִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּמּוֹתָר, וְאִם לָאו — טְעוּנָה גְּנִיזָה, חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁמָּא בְּלִבּוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם.
segments.en: The Gemara «raises an objection» from a baraita: In the case of «a gentile who donated a» cross «beam» and brought it to a synagogue, «and» the «name» of God «is written on it, one examines him» to determine his intent. «If he says: I separated it with» the «intent» that it be like the donations of «Jews,» the name should be «cut off [yagod]» and interred, «and one uses the remainder» for a synagogue. «And if not,» the entire beam «requires interment,» as «we are concerned» that «perhaps his heart was» directed «toward Heaven,» i.e., his intent was to consecrate it to the Temple, and therefore it may not be used.

segments.he: טַעְמָא דְּשֵׁם כָּתוּב עָלֶיהָ, דְּבָעֲיָא גְּנִיזָה; הָא אֵין שֵׁם כָּתוּב עָלֶיהָ — לָא בָּעֲיָא גְּנִיזָה!
segments.en: The Gemara analyzes this baraita: The «reason that» the beam «requires interment» is «that» the «name» of God «is written on it,» from which it may be inferred that if God’s «name» is «not written on it,» it «does not require interment.» Why, then, did Rav Yehuda say that if a gentile separated teruma it requires interment?

segments.he: הוּא הַדִּין דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּאֵין שֵׁם כָּתוּב עָלֶיהָ נָמֵי בָּעֲיָא גְּנִיזָה, וְהָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן, דְּאַף עַל גַּב דְּשֵׁם כָּתוּב עָלֶיהָ, יָגוֹד וְיִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּמּוֹתָר, דְּשֵׁם שֶׁלֹּא בִּמְקוֹמוֹ לָאו קָדוֹשׁ.
segments.en: The Gemara answers: «Even though» the «name» of God is «not written on» the beam, «the same» halakha «is true,» and the beam «requires interment,» due to the concern that he might have intended to consecrate it. «And» as for why the baraita specifically discusses the case where God’s name was written on the beam, «this teaches us that» if his intention was for it to be used in a synagogue, then «even though» God’s «name is written on it,» nevertheless the rest of the beam is not prohibited. Rather, the name should be «cut off» and interred, «and» one may «use the remainder» for a synagogue. The reason is «that» if God’s «name» is written on an item, only the place where it is written is sanctified, but that part of the item «that is not in its place is not sanctified.»

segments.he: דִּתְנַן: הָיָה כָּתוּב עַל יְדוֹת הַכֵּלִים וְעַל כַּרְעֵי הַמִּטָּה — הֲרֵי זֶה יָגוֹד וְיִגְנוֹז.
segments.en: «As we learned» in a baraita: If one of the names of God «was written on the handles of vessels or on legs of a bed, one must cut off» the name «and inter» it, and the remainder is permitted.

segments.he: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבָהוּ: הָאוֹמֵר ״סֶלַע זוֹ לִצְדָקָה״ — מוּתָּר לְשַׁנּוֹתָהּ. סְבוּר מִינַּהּ: לְעַצְמוֹ — אִין, לְאַחֵר — לָא. אִיתְּמַר: אָמַר רַב אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: בֵּין לְעַצְמוֹ בֵּין לְאַחֵר.
segments.en: § «Rav Naḥman says» that «Rabba bar Abbahu says: One who says:» I am contributing «this sela to charity, is permitted to change its» purpose, i.e., to use the money himself and later replace it. The Gemara comments: It was initially «understood from this» that if one wants to change its purpose «for his own» benefit, «yes,» this is permitted, as he originally had this stipulation in mind. But it is «not» permitted to lend it «to another.» Yet it «was stated» that «Rav Ami says» that «Rabbi Yoḥanan says:» It is permitted to change its purpose «whether for himself or for another.»

segments.he: אָמַר רַבִּי זְעֵירָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא דְּאָמַר ״עָלַי״, אֲבָל אָמַר ״הֲרֵי זוֹ״ — בְּעֵינַאּ בָּעֵי לְמִיתְּבַהּ.
segments.en: «Rabbi Zeira says: They taught» this halakha, that one may change the purpose of the coin, only in a case «where he said: It is» incumbent «upon me» to donate a sela to charity. «But» if he «said: This» sela «is» for charity, then he is «required to give» the sela to charity «as is,» and he may not use it and replace it.

segments.he: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רָבָא: אַדְּרַבָּה, אִיפְּכָא מִיסְתַּבְּרָא — אָמַר ״זוֹ״ מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בָּהּ, כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיחַיַּיב בְּאַחְרָיוּתַהּ, אֲבָל אָמַר ״עָלַי״ — לָא! אֶלָּא, לָא שְׁנָא.
segments.en: «Rava objects to this: On the contrary, the opposite is» more «reasonable.» In a case where one «said: This» sela is for charity, it makes sense to allow him to «use it, so that he should bear» financial «responsibility for its» loss from that point onward. «But» if he said: It is incumbent «upon me» to donate a sela to charity, he should «not» be allowed to use the sela, as in any event he must donate a sela. «Rather,» as there is a reason in either situation to permit its use, there «is no difference» between the cases, and in both cases he may use the sela.

moves.summary: Rav rules on a gentile who separated teruma: examine his intent, and where it is uncertain the produce is interred.
moves.about: a gentile who separated teruma from his pile is examined; with a Jew's intent it goes to a priest, otherwise it requires interment

moves.summary: Objects from a baraita about a gentile's donated beam bearing the divine name.
moves.about: a baraita requires interment of a gentile's donated beam only where God's name is written on it

moves.summary: Draws the limiting inference that without the name there is no interment, which would refute Rav.
moves.about: the baraita's stated reason implies that without the divine name on it the beam would need no interment, against Rav

moves.cueHe: הוא הדין דאף על גב דאין שם כתוב עליה
moves.summary: Rejects the inference: the case with the name was chosen to teach that a name out of its place is not sacred.
moves.about: the same law holds without the name too; the baraita's case teaches something else — that only the name's own place is sacred

moves.summary: Supports that answer from the ruling on a name written on vessel handles and bed legs.
moves.about: a ruling that a divine name written on vessel handles or bed legs is cut off and interred

moves.cueHe: אמר רב נחמן אמר רבה בר אבהו
moves.summary: One who pledges this sela to charity may divert its purpose.
moves.about: one who says this sela is for charity may divert it and replace it later

moves.summary: They first inferred that this permits diverting it for himself but not for another.
moves.about: they understood the permission to cover diverting the sela for himself only, not lending it to another

moves.summary: The received statement of R' Ami in R' Yoḥanan's name overturns that supposition: for himself or for another alike.
moves.about: brings R' Yoḥanan's ruling as the received statement against the supposition just floated

moves.cueHe: אמר רבי זעירא: לא שנו אלא
moves.summary: Limits the permission to one who said 'upon me', not one who said 'this sela'.
moves.about: the permission was taught only where he said the sela is upon me, not where he said this sela is for charity

moves.summary: Objects that the reasoning points the other way: 'this sela' is the case where use should be allowed.
moves.about: the opposite is more reasonable — saying 'this sela' should permit its use so that he bears responsibility for it, while 'upon me' should not

moves.summary: Concludes that the distinction collapses and both formulations permit use.
moves.about: since each formulation admits a reason to permit, the distinction collapses and the sela may be used in either case
